slides.say: Data Science from Scratch, lesson twelve: correlation is not causation.

slides.text: Two things that tend to move together
slides.say: Correlation means two things tend to move together. The most common measure, Pearson's r, runs from minus one to plus one. Plus one is a perfect positive straight-line link, minus one is a perfect negative one, and zero means no straight-line link.

slides.text: Moving together doesn't mean one causes the other
slides.say: The trap is assuming that because two things move together, one must cause the other. Correlation alone can't tell you that.

slides.text: A third factor can drive both
slides.sub: Ice cream sales and drownings both rise in hot weather
slides.say: Often a third factor drives both. A classic example: ice cream sales and drownings both rise in hot weather. Ice cream doesn't cause drowning. The heat drives both.

slides.text: The cause can run the other way
slides.sub: Failed payments lead to support calls, not the reverse
slides.say: Sometimes the cause runs the other way. Customers who call support more may have more failed payments. The calls probably don't cause the failures. The failures cause the calls.

slides.sub: Compare enough columns and some will line up
slides.say: And some correlations are just chance. If you compare enough columns, some will line up by coincidence.

slides.text: Correlation is a clue, not proof.
slides.sub: Testing cause usually needs an experiment
slides.say: So the takeaway: treat correlation as a clue, not proof. To test cause and effect, you usually need a controlled experiment, or a carefully designed study.

summary: Correlation measures how two variables move together (Pearson's r runs from -1 to +1), but it does not show cause. A hidden third factor, reverse causation or pure chance can all produce correlations; testing cause usually needs an experiment or careful study design.
practice: Think of two things that tend to rise together, for example umbrella sales and traffic jams. Write down a third factor that could drive both, then describe a simple comparison or experiment that could check whether one really causes the other.
